item.title: Maize Plant Height Estimation Using UAV and PlanetScope Imagery: A Comparison of 3-D Point Cloud and Machine Learning Approaches
item.description: Plant height (PH) is an essential indicator of crop growth and development, playing a critical role in field management and yield estimation. While recent advancements in remote sensing technologies have improved PH measurement capabilities, existing methods often encounter challenges related to accuracy, spatial resolution, and environmental conditions. In this study, we utilized low-altitude uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery and Planet satellite remote sensing data to explore PH measurement methods based on 3-D reconstructed point clouds and inversion from spectral and texture features. First, a 3-D point cloud method was used to generate a canopy height model (CHM) from a digital surface model (DSM) and a digital terrain model (DTM). Second, this study compared the accuracy of four machine learning methods: eXtreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), random forest (RF), partial least-squares regression (PLSR), and support vector regression (SVR), for PH inversion at the field scale. The results show that the direct 3-D point cloud method is the most accurate for PH estimation, achieving an $R^{2}$ of 0.98. For the machine learning inversion, the fusion of texture and spectral features consistently yielded the best performance for both data sources. Using high-resolution UAV imagery, XGBoost and RF models achieved the highest performance with an $R^{2}$ of 0.74. With 3-m PlanetScope imagery, the XGBoost model was the top performer, reaching a maximum $R^{2}$ of 0.59. On the contrary, the SVR model was consistently outperformed across all scenarios, highlighting the importance of appropriate model selection. Ultimately, high-resolution UAV imagery provided more accurate and reliable data for PH inversion compared to PlanetScope imagery. This study confirms the superiority of direct 3-D measurement and provides a clear guide for feature engineering and model selection in spectral-based PH estimation, providing new directions for future crop monitoring and precision agriculture research.
item.authors: Ke Li;Qing Li;Yanan Wei;Dalei Hao;Weijian Yu;Yelu Zeng;

item.title: Model, Source, and Analysis of BiSAR Maritime Moving Target’s Spatial Resolution
item.description: High-resolution imaging of maritime moving targets is of critical importance for maritime domain awareness and defense applications. Bistatic synthetic aperture radar (BiSAR) enables imaging for both stationary scenes and dynamic targets, where spatial resolution serves as a fundamental metric for system design and performance evaluation. While the resolution for static scenes can be derived from platform kinematics, it is invalid for moving targets owing to unknown translational motion and 3-D oscillations. Two fundamental limitations hinder current resolution analysis for moving targets: 1) direct application of such static-scene formulations to moving targets yields inaccurate resolution results, leading to failure of the system design; and 2) the resolution of moving targets depends on numerous factors, necessitating both quantitative and qualitative understanding of its statistical behavior. To address this issue, the resolution model and the physical source of BiSAR maritime moving targets have been systematically established and comprehensively characterized. First, the echo signal model of a maritime moving target in BiSAR is established, and the 2-D spatial resolution model is derived based on the gradient resolution theory. Subsequently, the azimuth resolution contribution index (ARCI) is proposed to quantitatively evaluate the individual contributions of the transmitter, receiver, and target motion to the azimuth resolution. Finally, a comprehensive analysis was carried out to investigate the time-varying characteristics of resolution and ARCI, as well as to analyze the impact of sea states, target rotation parameters, and platform configuration. The validity of the proposed ARCI and the derived theoretical framework is confirmed through numerical simulations.
